1:
The chapter opens with a group they recognise as such. Keil and Delitzsch note that the first three proverbs concern hearing and speaking, and a fourth follows which, like the second and third, turns on the soul. On the opening line they defend the Greek and Syriac rendering, a shrewd son obedient to his father: those translators read no different form but applied the Jewish rule that what is wanting is supplied from the context. Charles Ellicott offers a bolder alternative: a wise son is his father's instruction, the result and embodiment of it. Adam Clarke opens instead with a table of the chapter's topics.

On the mouth the readings run together. John Gill notes that the word his is not in the text, so the fruit may be another's mouth or one's own, the Greek reading the fruits of righteousness. Delitzsch explains why mouth and soul stand so close: speech is the most immediate and continuous expression of the soul. Matthew Henry wants a man who thinks twice before he speaks once, lays his hand on his lips to suppress an evil thought, and keeps a strong bridle on his tongue and a strict hand on that bridle. Clarke is blunter: the government of the tongue is a rare but useful talent, and men have often forfeited their lives by treasonable words.

The sluggard is described alike by three and turned inward by the fourth. Gill has him desire knowledge without pains, riches without industry, fine clothing without labour, so that he goes in rags. Henry catches the absurdity: they desire the gains the diligent get but hate the pains the diligent take. Delitzsch adds only that the soul of the industrious is richly satisfied. Clarke applies it to religion, where men desire more of the divine life and never get forward, because they do not stir themselves up to lay hold upon the Lord, always learning and never coming to the knowledge of the truth.

The hatred of lying is taken broadly. Gill lists the kinds hated: lies in common conversation, religious lies, doctrinal lies, lies spoken in hypocrisy. Henry generalises further, since every sin is a lie, so the righteous man not only will not tell one but abhors lying from a rooted principle. Ellicott is uncertain about the second clause: the wicked man is loathsome, or disgraces and shames by his calumnies, or simply acts basely. Delitzsch finds the next verse almost enigmatically expressed, while Henry has integrity keep the upright from Satan's temptations.

The two kinds of pretence are matched. Delitzsch gives the pair as one who makes himself rich and has nothing, another who represents himself poor amid great riches, both verbs reflexive. Clarke names them: the former is the rich poor man, the latter the poor rich man, illustrated from the dog in the manger and from the apostle who was as poor yet making many rich. Henry describes men who trade and spend as if they had hidden treasure when, their debts paid, they are not worth a groat. Gill finds the same pretence among hypocrites who would be thought rich in grace.

The ransom verse divides on who is better off. Ellicott says the rich man may have to give all to save his life, while the poor need not regard a threat, his insignificance being his protection. Clarke localises it: in despotic countries a rich man is accused of a capital crime and must buy his life though innocent, while the poor are put to no trouble. John Wesley gives the poor two reasons for safety: they are cautious not to provoke others, and are esteemed objects of pity. Delitzsch corrects a scholar who took the clause of warning, since the contrast points to a threat against life. Henry draws the moral: we judge blessedness by wealth, and Solomon shows what a gross mistake that is.
9:
The light and the lamp are distinguished. Charles Ellicott draws the difference out: the righteous walks in the light of God's truth, his path becoming ever more plain, the other by the glimmer of his own lamp. Adam Clarke reads both as posterity: the righteous have a joyous line, the wicked's is cut off. Matthew Henry keeps it inward, making the Spirit their light; John Wesley keeps it outward, prosperity whose end is hidden.

On pride the agreement is total, the grammar disputed. Keil and Delitzsch say the restrictive particle belongs not to pride but to contention, so nothing comes by pride but contention; Ellicott agrees. John Gill offers an alternative: an empty man through pride will make contention, since those emptiest of knowledge are proudest. Henry calls foolish pride the great make-bate: whatever hand passion or envy may have in a quarrel, pride has the great hand, sowing discord itself and needing no help. Clarke extends it: perhaps no quarrel in private life and no war among nations does not proceed from pride, since neither man nor nation will be less than another.

Wealth gotten by vanity is defined by method. Gill lists them: robbery, fraud, cards and dice and stage playing, and the illicit arts of necromancy and judicial astrology. Clarke names modern equivalents: fortunes from speculation, lucky hits, and ministering to others' pride or luxury, soon dissipated because not gotten in the way of providence. Henry has it that riches wear as they are won and woven, since the dispositions that incline men to sinful getting incline them to sinful spending. Ellicott glosses it as dishonesty.

Hope deferred is analysed, not illustrated. Clarke traces the sequence: a good is discovered, its want felt, desire excited, the promise made on grounds not to be suspected, so hope posts forward, and delay pains the mind. Henry makes the distinction that matters: the grief is not a denial but a delay; hope deferred makes the heart sick, hope quite dashed kills it outright, and the higher the expectation the more cutting the frustration. Gill has the heart sink and fail. Delitzsch notices that the paradise figures here and two verses later require the verse between to be read with both.

Despising the word gets two senses. Delitzsch renders it that whoever despises the word is in bonds to it, the word being an ordering commandment. Ellicott allows both, that the despiser brings ruin on himself, or is still bound to the word while neglecting it, and compares the counsel to agree with an adversary quickly. Gill takes the word for Christ himself, despised in those who despise his ministers. On the law of the wise, Clarke would translate that the law is to the wise man a fountain of life, the same to him as the artery carrying blood from the heart through the body. Ellicott prefers instruction to law, and traces the snares of death to the devil.

The last group is bound by sound, not sense. Delitzsch observes that four proverbs here appear connected by the likeness of their words, and calls the way of the malicious uncultivated. Ellicott makes it rough and barren, against the green pastures and still waters of the psalm. Clarke's comment on that line is the sharpest in the chapter: never was a truer saying, since most sinners have more pain and difficulty to get their souls damned than the righteous have, with all their cross-bearings, to reach heaven. Wesley calls the way offensive and hateful, as rough ways are to a traveller. Henry has the prudent man consult others and refuse to meddle with what he does not know. On the messenger Clarke reports that the Greek read a bold king in its place; Ellicott adds that the faithless one brings down those who sent him, a faithful one being health to himself and his employers.
18:
Refusing instruction is read as pride before loss. Matthew Henry has the man who scorns to be taught refuse good offered him as a slight on his honour and a curb on his liberty. John Gill carries the poverty and shame into the next world. Charles Ellicott gives the verse on desire two constructions: either the fools' clinging to evil prevents them attaining what is worth desiring, or, reading the particle as therefore, they give up nothing they have set their minds on, however evil. John Wesley takes the second, since sinners rejoice in the satisfaction of their lusts and abhor all restraint.

On company the agreement is complete. Adam Clarke says that to walk with a person implies love, and it is impossible not to imitate those we love: show me his company and I will tell you the man. Henry says a man's character is known by the company he chooses and formed by it. Keil and Delitzsch render the second line that whoever has intercourse with fools becomes base, and Ellicott glosses the destruction as moral ruin. Gill has the growth come by frequent private conversation.

The pursuit of sinners draws three images. Delitzsch says the verb is of a punishment following sinners at their heels, and remarks that Greek art gives wings to Nemesis in the same sense. Henry has evil pursue them as the avenger of blood pursued the manslayer, with no city of refuge, since whom God pursues he overtakes. Ellicott sets the snares and fire and brimstone of one psalm against the good measure, pressed down and running over, awaiting the righteous.

The inheritance verse is read morally, not economically. Ellicott notices that the good man answers to the just man of the next line, so the word probably means liberal or unselfish. Clarke makes the legacy partly immaterial: the good man files many a prayer in heaven for them, and his example and advices are remembered from generation to generation, while what property he left was honestly acquired and therefore permanent, ill-gotten property seldom reaching the third generation, as even the heathens observed.

On the poor man's tillage they part over who is blamed. Ellicott takes the field for newly broken ground on which much labour has been spent, so the poor hardworking man gains an abundant living while many rich are ruined for neglecting what is right. Delitzsch renders it much the same, that many are destroyed by iniquity. Henry answers the excuse that a man has little to work on: the smaller the field the more skill it deserves. Clarke turns the second clause against the poor themselves: much of their poverty arises from want of management, since they have little economy and no foresight, and speedily spend whatever they get, so a feast and a famine make the chief varieties of their life. Wesley keeps to the first clause, where diligence and blessing often make poor men rich.

The rod is defended and then defined. Gill says such fond love as spares it is no better than hatred: a father who really hated his son could scarcely do him a worse turn. Henry insists on whose rod it is: every child of ours is a child of Adam, with that foolishness bound up in its heart which calls for rebuke, but it must be a parent's rod, directed by wisdom and love and designed for good, not a servant's. On the closing verse Henry finds the happiness of the righteous in having enough and knowing when they have it, since nature is content with a little and grace with less; Clarke adds that the wicked, though he stick not at rapine, is often in real want and always dissatisfied: a contented mind is a continual feast at which he never eats. Delitzsch denies that the verse commends temperance at all.
